title: LRU Variants
description: Explore LFU cache, Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC), size-aware eviction, distributed LRU with consistent hashing, and Caffeine cache internals.

segments.text: LRU has a blind spot: frequency. A one-time full table scan evicts all your hot cached items. LRU only tracks recency, not how frequently items are accessed. In production, this causes cache pollution — one bad query destroys cache hit rates. That's why real systems use LRU variants.

LFU — Least Frequently Used — evicts items with the lowest access count. A hot key accessed a million times won't be evicted by a scan. But LFU has cache aging problems — an item popular last week keeps high counts even if nobody accesses it now. The solution: decay counters over time or use a windowed frequency count.

IBM's Adaptive Replacement Cache combines LRU and LFU dynamically. It maintains four lists: recent items, frequent items, and ghost lists for recently evicted items from each category. If a ghost-recent hit occurs, ARC grows the recent portion. If a ghost-frequent hit occurs, it grows the frequent portion. Self-tuning without configuration.

Standard LRU treats all items equally — a one-kilobyte item and a one-megabyte item both count as one eviction unit. Size-aware eviction considers item size. The cost function becomes: value divided by size. A frequently accessed one-kilobyte item is worth keeping over a rarely accessed one-megabyte item. Varnish cache uses size-aware eviction.

Your cache has a one-gigabyte capacity. You have two types of items: ten-kilobyte items accessed one hundred times per second, and ten-megabyte items accessed once per second. How do you maximize cache hit rate?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you balance caching small-hot items vs large-cold items in a fixed-size cache?

segments.text: Distributed LRU partitions the cache across nodes using consistent hashing. Key 'user:42' always goes to node three. Each node runs its own local LRU. The consistent hashing ring ensures even distribution and minimal disruption when nodes join or leave. Memcached and Redis Cluster work exactly this way.

Caffeine is the state-of-the-art JVM cache. It uses Window TinyLFU — a small admission window of one percent LRU combined with ninety-nine percent Segmented LFU as the main space. New items enter the window. If evicted from the window but have high frequency, they're admitted to the main space. This outperforms pure LRU by fifteen to thirty percent in hit rate.

TinyLFU uses a Count-Min Sketch to track frequency in constant space. Four bits per counter with periodic halving for aging. The entire frequency tracking structure for millions of keys fits in kilobytes of memory. This is how Caffeine achieves near-optimal hit rates without the memory overhead of exact frequency counts.

Write policies affect cache behavior significantly. Write-through: write to cache and backing store simultaneously — consistent but slow. Write-back: write to cache only, flush to backing store later — fast but risk of data loss. Write-around: write to backing store only, cache on next read — prevents cache pollution from write-heavy workloads.

You're designing a cache for a CDN edge server. Items range from one kilobyte to one hundred megabytes. Access patterns are Zipf-distributed. Total cache capacity is fifty gigabytes. Which eviction policy and data structures would you choose?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a CDN edge cache: 50GB, items 1KB-100MB, Zipf access. What eviction policy?

segments.text: LRU variants solve real-world caching problems that vanilla LRU cannot. LFU handles frequency, ARC self-tunes between recency and frequency, size-aware eviction optimizes memory utilization, and Caffeine's Window TinyLFU achieves near-optimal hit rates. The Staff-level insight: choosing the right eviction policy requires understanding your access pattern — measure before deciding.
